en: The Story of Daṇḍin:
In a certain country, there lived a certain Brahmin known by the name Daṇḍin.
He became utterly dejected, deprived of food;
he also became deprived of garments.
From a certain householder, he [obtained] a bull.
Someone was hired.
During the day, he yoked the bull to work and then, taking it with him,
went to the house of that householder.
There in that house, the householder was indeed enjoying his meal;
meanwhile, that bull had been released by Daṇḍin into the middle of the courtyard of the residence.
The bull, having passed through another doorway, disappeared. That householder, too, having eaten that meal, rose up;
and not seeing the bull there in the courtyard of the house, he asked a staff-bearer, "Where is the bull?"
The staff-bearer replied, "He was released in your house.
The householder spoke again, "Since you abandoned my bull, you must restore it to me.
The staff-bearer answered, "I did not destroy the ox."
Then the two of them said, "Let us go together into the presence of the king;
he will investigate our case for its justice or injustice," and having spoken thus, they set out.
At that time, a certain horse belonging to another person, having broken its tether, bolted away.
The man [standing among the people] asked the staff-bearer, "Where is my horse?
The staff-bearer replied, "I did not [bind it like a bull]; nor was the horse [released from its tether].
Thereupon, that staff-bearer took up a certain stone for the purpose of striking down the horse and hurled it at the horse.
That stone, having struck a single hoof of the mare, shattered it.
Thereupon, that person said: "Since you have killed my horse, give me back my horse!
[The staff-bearer replied: "For what reason should I give you the horse?"
He was summoned by that person: "Come here;
let us go into the presence of the king. He will bring our deliberation to its conclusion."
Then the two of them departed.
[Out of fear of his enemies] that staff-bearer began to flee.
[At the moment of retreat] he leaped down beneath a certain wall.
In front of him sat a certain weaver weaving threads. A staff fell upon that weaver, and he died.
Then the weaver’s wife seized Daṇḍin by the hand.
She said, “Since you have killed my husband, give me back my husband!
Daṇḍin replied, “How can I restore your master to you?”
He said, "Come this way;
let us go into the presence of the king. He will settle our dispute. Then the two of them went.
In the middle of their path, there was a certain deep river.
On its bank, facing the water, a certain carpenter arrived carrying an axe in his mouth. He was questioned by Daṇḍin: "How deep is the water?"
By saying, "The water is deep," the carpenter’s axe fell into the water;
he could not find his axe,
and so the carpenter remained there with the handle in his hand.
[The Sūtradhāra reproached him: "You have cast my axe into the water! To this, the Daṇḍin replied: "I did not throw it. [The Sūtradhāra said: "Come here!"
"Let us go into the presence of the king; he will provide a decision for us," they said, and having spoken thus, the two departed.
Then they all went and arrived in the presence of the lord of men;
they bowed their heads at the feet of the king.
They sat down on one side.
Then the king asked them, "For what purpose have you come?
Thereupon, they all explained to the king the dispute between Daṇḍin and the householder.
[Having heard that explanation] the King said to Daṇḍin: "Did you carry off a bull? [Daṇḍin took up the word: "Indeed so.
[The King said:
"Then restore it!"
“[Do so] such that the bull is seen by the householder at the time of repayment,” [he said].
Daṇḍin replied, “Indeed, the bull was not handed over to the householder with a formal address.
The king proclaimed, “Since this Daṇḍin, without even addressing him, [returned the bull]...”
"Cut off his tongue because he gave it away;
and since the master of the house did not tie up the bull even though he saw it coming, pluck out one of his eyes."
The householder said: "First, my bull was destroyed by Daṇḍin;
secondly, my eyes were plucked out. Therefore, it is better that in this dispute, Daṇḍin alone should be the victor.
Then a certain person [the owner of horses] said: "Your Majesty, my horses have been killed by Daṇḍin."
The king asked Daṇḍin, "How were the horses killed by you?
Daṇḍin replied, "When I set out on the road, the horses arrived.
This person did not release the horses from their bonds; therefore, they arrived having broken their own bonds."
“I took up a certain stone for the purpose of stopping her speed; having exhausted that stone, she was struck down by me,” he said.
The king replied, “Since Aśvapati did not release the horse from its bonds, cut his girth.”
"Daṇḍin has thrown a stone; cut off one of his arms!
Thus was it said by that man, the lord of the steeds: "First, my horse was killed."
"Rather than my tongue being cut off for a second time, let the victor be punished by the staff!
[Then] the weaver's wife said: "My husband has been struck by the staff-bearer!"
Daṇḍin informed [the king]: "Terrified that my enemies had increased, I leaped over the wall and fled;
while doing so, a person sitting in the middle [a weaver] was killed without being seen.
The king said: "Go then,"
“[Daṇḍin,] become the husband of this very woman,” she was told by that weaver’s wife: “First, my own master died.”
"Since this fool will become my husband, it would be better if the winner were Daṇḍin himself," [she said in her decision].
Then the Sūtradhāra declared: "Because Daṇḍin asked me, 'How deep is the water? the axe held in my mouth fell into the water."
The king said: "Since it is appropriate for one carrying even the slightest object on his shoulder to bear an axe in his mouth, first break the two tusks of this stage-manager.
Since he asked, 'Is there any depth to the water?', cut out his tongue."
Then the stage-manager said: "First my axe was lost; thus they all each performed their respective deliberations and reached their conclusions.
And the staff-bearer was released from all charges."
